title: Well and Portrait
premise: Elodie Quintana takes a teaching post in the isolated village of Hollowmere, where children vanish from class rosters and no one will say their names. The village church bell—melted down in 1911 after a drowning scandal—begins ringing at night, and Elodie's meticulous documentation reveals a pattern: every disappearance matches an entry in a founder's ledger of debts. The founders bound something beneath the old well with a ritual that requires thirteen named sacrifices per century, and this generation's tithe is due. To save the remaining students, Elodie must complete or break the founders' unfinished rite, choosing between the village's survival and their own conscience; they end it by giving the well a name instead of bodies, freeing the drowned dead but shattering Hollowmere's founding lie.
about_author: C. M. Nystrom is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent nine years in villages too small for maps. They write horror about records, rituals, and the violence small communities commit to stay whole.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Arriving in Hollowmere, they unpack boxes of notebooks and begin documenting everything: the school, the fog, the way villagers count children twice. The class roster lists twelve students; only nine appear. Emotional beat: cautious hope curdling into quiet unease.

chapters.title: The Roster Problem
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Three seats sit empty all week. When Elodie asks the headmaster, Mr. Voss, he says the missing children are 'away at family,' but their coats still hang on hooks. Beat: the first crack in the village's polite surface.

chapters.title: Bell Metal
chapters.summary: Village archivist Marta's POV. Marta shows Elodie the parish record: the bell was melted in 1911 after the Quintana-adjacent drowning of two founders' sons. She warns Elodie to stop writing things down. Beat: dread disguised as kindness.

chapters.title: First Ringing
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. At 3 a.m. the church bell rings though there is no bell. Elodie photographs the empty tower; the photo shows rope marks and wet stone. Beat: terror meeting the comfort of evidence.

chapters.title: Nine Names
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Cross-referencing a century of school ledgers, Elodie finds that every third year, exactly four names vanish mid-term—and the entries are written in the same hand across decades. Beat: obsessive clarity, the prayer of documentation working.

chapters.title: The Well Behind the School
chapters.summary: Student POV—Wren, age eleven. Wren leads Elodie to the capped well behind the playground and admits she hears her vanished brother calling from it. Beat: a child's matter-of-fact horror breaking Elodie's composure.

chapters.title: Ledger of Debts
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. Marta finally opens the founders' ledger: thirteen names per century, 'paid' to keep the well sealed. Her own grandmother's signature is there. Beat: inherited guilt and complicity.

chapters.title: What Voss Knows
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Confronting Voss, Elodie learns he was a listed name as a boy, spared when another child was taken in his place. He begs Elodie to leave before the tithe completes. Beat: pity warring with fury.

chapters.title: The Drowned Choir
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren follows the singing to the well at night and sees faces in the water—children from 1911, still waiting to be counted present. Beat: heartbreak; the dead are not monsters, only unrecorded.

chapters.title: Ritual Fragments
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. In the founders' chapel crypt, Elodie finds the rite half-burned: it requires thirteen names spoken over the water by someone who 'owes nothing.' Elodie owes nothing—but finishing it might seal the next hundred years. Beat: moral vertigo.

chapters.title: Intermission of Fog
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. A false calm; the village prepares its autumn festival as if nothing is wrong. Marta burns part of the ledger and immediately regrets it. Beat: the terrible ordinariness of complicity.

chapters.title: Tenth Name
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. A student stops coming to school; the coat remains. The bell rings ten times now. Elodie realizes the count is public arithmetic—the village can hear how close it is. Beat: countdown dread.

chapters.title: The Founders' Sons
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV via recovered letters. The 1911 drowning wasn't accident: the founders sacrificed their own sons first to start the debt, believing grief would sanctify it. Beat: revelation that the village was founded on a crime.

chapters.title: Wren Is Listed
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie finds Wren's name inked fresh in the ledger, dated three days hence. Voss confesses the village council wrote it. Beat: love against duty crystallizes—Elodie must choose the child over the town.

chapters.title: Council of Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. The council votes to let the tithe proceed; Marta abstains, then walks out. On the steps she gives Elodie the one page she saved. Beat: defection; justice begins outside the law.

chapters.title: Thirteen Bells
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Taken to the well at midnight, Wren sings back to the drowned children rather than cry. The bell rings thirteen times and stops mid-stroke. Beat: courage in the smallest voice.

chapters.title: The Unfinished Rite
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie interrupts the ceremony, seizes the ledger, and speaks the drowned children's true names over the water instead of Wren's—naming the dead releases them. The well exhales a century of fog. Beat: climax; documentation becomes liberation.

chapters.title: What Rose From the Water
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs braided. The freed dead walk through the village touching doorframes, reading their own names aloud from Elodie's notebooks. Some villagers kneel; some flee. Beat: awe and reckoning entwined.

chapters.title: The Bell Recast
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. The melted bell's bronze is found whole in the tower, cold and wet. It rings once, by itself—a roll call answered. Beat: mourning turning toward peace.

chapters.title: Trials Without Law
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. With no legal authority for miles, the village must judge itself; Elodie reads the ledger aloud as evidence while the councilors stand in the square. Beat: justice outside the law, administered through testimony.

chapters.title: Present, All Present
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Spring term: the roster holds thirteen names, all attending—including, some mornings, faint chalk handwriting adding itself. Wren answers 'here' for her brother once. Beat: grief integrated, tenderness amid strangeness.

chapters.title: Well and Portrait
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie seals the well with a stone carved with every name and hangs a portrait of the founders' sons beside it—not honored, but witnessed. Closing the last notebook, Elodie stays on as teacher. Beat: resolution; memory kept without debt.
